BOFAH Chapter 16








In our theory of growth we argued two things:

Only growth in productivity can improve income per worker, permanently.
Transition towards steady state capital via capital accumulation induces temporary growth.

Adam Smith argued that the invisible hand maximizes welfare because:

it incentivizes specialisation of labour
it incentivizes free trade, expanding consumption possibilities







Source: World Bank; Our World in Data
Trade = Exports + Imports. This ratio proxies how integrated the global economy is.





Why do countries trade?
Differences in:

technologies and endowments
consumer tastes

Countries:

specialize in relatively efficient production
export those goods
import others

We study the Ricardian model (technology differences)








Two sectors: Manufacturing (\(m\)), Services (\(s\))

\[
Y_m = A_m L_m \qquad Y_s = A_s L_s
\]

Labour constraint:

\[

\]
Rearrange:

\]




\[

\]

Intercept: \(A_s L\)
Slope (opportunity cost):

\[
\frac{dY_s}{dY_m} = -\frac{A_s}{A_m}
\]

title: Tracking the Modern Macroeconomy: Key Data Releases Economists Watch Closely
text:
Macroeconomics has increasingly become a “high-frequency” discipline. Financial markets, central banks, journalists, and economists now react almost immediately to incoming economic data. Certain statistics — especially in the United States — have become highly influential because they provide rapid signals about inflation, employment, growth, and monetary policy.
The growing popularity of these data releases reflects three developments:
Below are some of the most closely watched macroeconomic indicators in modern macroeconomics.

title: Tracking the Modern Macroeconomy: Key Data Releases Economists Watch Closely
text:
Release Window

Released monthly
Usually the first Friday of every month
Published by the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS)

title: Tracking the Modern Macroeconomy: Key Data Releases Economists Watch Closely
text:
What It Measures

Employment growth
Unemployment rate
Wage growth
Labor force participation

title: Tracking the Modern Macroeconomy: Key Data Releases Economists Watch Closely
text:
Why It Became Popular
The jobs report became central because the Federal Reserve increasingly emphasized “maximum employment” as part of its dual mandate. After the 2008 financial crisis and again after COVID-19, labor market conditions became the main guide for monetary policy decisions.
Financial markets also realized that labor market tightness strongly predicts future inflationary pressure through wage growth.

title: Tracking the Modern Macroeconomy: Key Data Releases Economists Watch Closely
text:
Benefits of Tracking It
Economists use it to: - Gauge recession risk - Measure labor market tightness - Infer inflationary pressures - Predict Federal Reserve policy decisions - Assess household income growth and consumption strength

title: Tracking the Modern Macroeconomy: Key Data Releases Economists Watch Closely
text:
Main Weakness
The report is volatile and subject to revisions.

title: Tracking the Modern Macroeconomy: Key Data Releases Economists Watch Closely
text:
Release Window

Released monthly
Usually around the middle of the month
Published by the BLS

title: Tracking the Modern Macroeconomy: Key Data Releases Economists Watch Closely
text:
What It Measures

Inflation faced by households
Prices of goods and services

title: Tracking the Modern Macroeconomy: Key Data Releases Economists Watch Closely
text:
Why It Became Popular
Inflation was relatively stable from the mid-1990s to around 2020, so CPI attracted less public attention during the “Great Moderation.” However, the post-pandemic inflation surge made CPI one of the most watched statistics globally.
Markets now react intensely to “inflation surprises” because they alter expectations of future interest rates.

title: Tracking the Modern Macroeconomy: Key Data Releases Economists Watch Closely
text:
Benefits of Tracking It
Economists use CPI to: - Measure inflation persistence - Study real wage growth - Estimate cost-of-living changes - Forecast monetary policy tightening or easing

title: Tracking the Modern Macroeconomy: Key Data Releases Economists Watch Closely
text:
Main Weakness
Headline CPI can be heavily influenced by volatile food and energy prices.

title: Tracking the Modern Macroeconomy: Key Data Releases Economists Watch Closely
text:
Release Window

Released monthly
Published by the Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA)

title: Tracking the Modern Macroeconomy: Key Data Releases Economists Watch Closely
text:
What It Measures

Inflation excluding food and energy
Personal consumption expenditures price index

title: Tracking the Modern Macroeconomy: Key Data Releases Economists Watch Closely
text:
Why It Became Popular
The Federal Reserve officially prefers Core PCE over CPI because: - It better captures substitution behavior - It has broader expenditure coverage - It is viewed as a cleaner measure of underlying inflation trends
As Fed communication became more transparent, economists increasingly focused on whichever inflation measure the Fed itself emphasized.

title: Tracking the Modern Macroeconomy: Key Data Releases Economists Watch Closely
text:
Benefits of Tracking It
Useful for: - Understanding trend inflation - Predicting Fed behavior - Filtering temporary price shocks

title: Tracking the Modern Macroeconomy: Key Data Releases Economists Watch Closely
text:
Main Weakness
Less intuitive for the general public than CPI.

title: Tracking the Modern Macroeconomy: Key Data Releases Economists Watch Closely
text:
Release Window

Eight scheduled meetings per year
Announced by the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC)

title: Tracking the Modern Macroeconomy: Key Data Releases Economists Watch Closely
text:
What It Measures

The Federal Reserve’s policy interest rate

title: Tracking the Modern Macroeconomy: Key Data Releases Economists Watch Closely
text:
Why It Became Popular
Modern macroeconomics increasingly views monetary policy as the central stabilization tool of the economy. Since financial markets price assets based on expected future interest rates, every Fed decision has major implications for: - Bonds - Equity markets - Exchange rates - Housing markets
Fed communication itself has become an economic event.

title: Tracking the Modern Macroeconomy: Key Data Releases Economists Watch Closely
text:
Benefits of Tracking It
Economists use it to: - Infer the stance of monetary policy - Estimate recession probabilities - Understand financial conditions - Study transmission of monetary shocks

title: Tracking the Modern Macroeconomy: Key Data Releases Economists Watch Closely
text:
Main Weakness
Markets often care more about future guidance than the current rate itself.

title: Tracking the Modern Macroeconomy: Key Data Releases Economists Watch Closely
text:
Release Window

Quarterly
Advance estimate released roughly one month after quarter end
Published by the BEA

title: Tracking the Modern Macroeconomy: Key Data Releases Economists Watch Closely
text:
What It Measures

Total output of the economy

title: Tracking the Modern Macroeconomy: Key Data Releases Economists Watch Closely
text:
Why It Became Popular
GDP remains the broadest measure of aggregate economic activity and is still the standard measure of economic growth.
However, because GDP is released with delays, markets increasingly rely on “nowcasting” using higher-frequency indicators.

title: Tracking the Modern Macroeconomy: Key Data Releases Economists Watch Closely
text:
Benefits of Tracking It
Useful for: - Dating recessions - Measuring economic growth - Cross-country comparisons - Productivity analysis

title: Tracking the Modern Macroeconomy: Key Data Releases Economists Watch Closely
text:
Main Weakness
Released slowly and heavily revised later.

title: Tracking the Modern Macroeconomy: Key Data Releases Economists Watch Closely
text:
Release Window

Weekly
Released every Thursday

title: Tracking the Modern Macroeconomy: Key Data Releases Economists Watch Closely
text:
What It Measures

Number of people filing unemployment insurance claims

title: Tracking the Modern Macroeconomy: Key Data Releases Economists Watch Closely
text:
Why It Became Popular
Economists increasingly value high-frequency data because it gives faster information than monthly or quarterly releases. Initial claims became especially important during crises such as: - 2008 financial crisis - COVID-19 recession
It provides one of the fastest signals of labor market deterioration.

title: Tracking the Modern Macroeconomy: Key Data Releases Economists Watch Closely
text:
Benefits of Tracking It
Useful for: - Detecting turning points - Monitoring recession risk in real time - Measuring layoffs

title: Tracking the Modern Macroeconomy: Key Data Releases Economists Watch Closely
text:
Main Weakness
Very noisy week-to-week.

title: Tracking the Modern Macroeconomy: Key Data Releases Economists Watch Closely
text:
Release Window

Continuously available in financial markets

title: Tracking the Modern Macroeconomy: Key Data Releases Economists Watch Closely
text:
What It Measures

Difference between long-term and short-term interest rates

title: Tracking the Modern Macroeconomy: Key Data Releases Economists Watch Closely
text:
Why It Became Popular
Yield curve inversion became famous because it historically predicted many U.S. recessions.
Modern macroeconomics increasingly incorporates financial markets into business cycle analysis, making bond market indicators highly influential.

title: Tracking the Modern Macroeconomy: Key Data Releases Economists Watch Closely
text:
Benefits of Tracking It
Useful for: - Predicting recessions - Understanding market expectations - Measuring expected future monetary policy

title: Tracking the Modern Macroeconomy: Key Data Releases Economists Watch Closely
text:
Main Weakness
Structural changes in bond markets may weaken predictive power.

title: Tracking the Modern Macroeconomy: Key Data Releases Economists Watch Closely
text:
Release Window

Monthly
Released very early each month

title: Tracking the Modern Macroeconomy: Key Data Releases Economists Watch Closely
text:
What It Measures

Business sentiment
Manufacturing and services activity

title: Tracking the Modern Macroeconomy: Key Data Releases Economists Watch Closely
text:
Why It Became Popular
Markets value PMI because it arrives earlier than most “hard” economic data. It acts as an early indicator of: - Production - Demand - Employment intentions

title: Tracking the Modern Macroeconomy: Key Data Releases Economists Watch Closely
text:
Benefits of Tracking It
Useful for: - Short-run forecasting - Tracking business cycle momentum - Identifying turning points

title: Tracking the Modern Macroeconomy: Key Data Releases Economists Watch Closely
text:
Main Weakness
It measures sentiment rather than actual output.

title: Tracking the Modern Macroeconomy: Key Data Releases Economists Watch Closely
text:
Release Window

Monthly
Published by the U.S. Census Bureau

title: Tracking the Modern Macroeconomy: Key Data Releases Economists Watch Closely
text:
What It Measures

Consumer spending activity

title: Tracking the Modern Macroeconomy: Key Data Releases Economists Watch Closely
text:
Why It Became Popular
Consumption is roughly 70% of U.S. GDP, so retail sales provide rapid information about aggregate demand strength.

title: Tracking the Modern Macroeconomy: Key Data Releases Economists Watch Closely
text:
Benefits of Tracking It
Useful for: - Forecasting GDP - Measuring consumer confidence indirectly - Assessing household demand

title: Tracking the Modern Macroeconomy: Key Data Releases Economists Watch Closely
text:
Main Weakness
Excludes many services expenditures.

title: Tracking the Modern Macroeconomy: Key Data Releases Economists Watch Closely
text:
Release Window

Monthly

title: Tracking the Modern Macroeconomy: Key Data Releases Economists Watch Closely
text:
What It Measures

Construction activity
Housing market turnover

title: Tracking the Modern Macroeconomy: Key Data Releases Economists Watch Closely
text:
Why It Became Popular
Housing is highly interest-sensitive and therefore reacts strongly to monetary policy changes.
Because housing often turns before the broader economy, economists use it as a leading indicator.

title: Tracking the Modern Macroeconomy: Key Data Releases Economists Watch Closely
text:
Benefits of Tracking It
Useful for: - Measuring monetary policy transmission - Forecasting construction employment - Understanding household balance sheet conditions

title: Tracking the Modern Macroeconomy: Key Data Releases Economists Watch Closely
text:
Main Weakness
Sensitive to weather and seasonality.

title: Economics of Growth: Thoughts on the Evolution of the Literature
text:
If you look at growth literature, the citations to these papers are very high. There is a “level effect” to citation within these papers i.e. these papers are of the order of 40K magnitude while key papers in business cycle theory is 10K. The reason for this is the general and global reach of the growth literature especially since it handles big questions.
I also find that as one goes deep into the issue, the mass citation that earlier ideas gathered has withered away. My intuition about this is that as the literature flourishes, new strands with fresh ideas have an explosion effect. But as and when the literature matures, the new ideas are more incremental and hence the citations are more spread out. You can see this in papers by Acemoglou (Directed Technical Change) where he is pushing the endogenous growth literature in a certain direction, but is not catching up to gain momentum and is viewed as important but not explosive.
The recent discussion in the backdrop of thing literature is even more interesting. On one hand the discussion is getting into nitty gritty of the productivity measurement debate through the lens of misallocation. On the other hand, new aspects of this debate are making way partly due to the evolution of the economies themselves. For instance, the discussion on the role of ideas in growth and the implications of a declining population on growth are very recent and interesting.
I read about the quote by Lucas


Solow, R. M. (1956). A contribution to the theory of economic growth. The quarterly journal of economics, 70(1), 65-94.
Cass, D. (1965). Optimum growth in an aggregative model of capital accumulation. The Review of economic studies, 32(3), 233-240.
Cass, D. (1966). Optimum growth in an aggregative model of capital accumulation: A turnpike theorem. Econometrica: Journal of the Econometric Society, 833-850.
Koopmans, Tjalling C., “On the Concept of Optimal Economic Growth” (1963). Cowles Foundation Discussion Papers. 392.
Romer, P. M. (1986). Increasing returns and long-run growth. Journal of political economy, 94(5), 1002-1037.
R. E. Lucas Jr. On the mechanics of economic development. Journal of monetary economics, 22(1):3–42, July 1988.
Romer, P. M. (1990). Endogenous technological change. Journal of political Economy, 98(5, Part 2), S71-S102.
Barro, R. J. (1991). Economic growth in a cross section of countries. The quarterly journal of economics, 106(2), 407-443.
Mankiw, N. G., Romer, D., & Weil, D. N. (1992). A contribution to the empirics of economic growth. The quarterly journal of economics, 107(2), 407-437.
Levine, R., & Renelt, D. (1992). A sensitivity analysis of cross-country growth regressions. The American economic review, 942-963.
Barro, R. J., & Sala-i-Martin, X. (1992). Convergence. Journal of political Economy, 100(2), 223-251.
Aghion, P., & Howitt, P. (1992). A Model of Growth Through Creative Destruction. Econometrica: Journal of the Econometric Society, 323-351.
Klenow, P. J., & Rodriguez-Clare, A. (1997). The neoclassical revival in growth economics: Has it gone too far?. NBER macroeconomics annual, 12, 73-103.


The neoclassical (Solow-style) model, when properly interpreted, can explain most cross-country income differences—you do not need strong endogenous growth mechanisms.


Hall, R. E., & Jones, C. I. (1999). Why do some countries produce so much more output per worker than others?. The quarterly journal of economics, 114(1), 83-116.
Jones, C. I. (2016). The facts of economic growth. In Handbook of macroeconomics (Vol. 2, pp. 3-69). Elsevier. following up from: Jones, C. I. (2002). Sources of US economic growth in a world of ideas. American economic review, 92(1), 220-239.
Jones, C. I. (2022). The end of economic growth? Unintended consequences of a declining population. American Economic Review, 112(11), 3489-3527.
Jones, C. I. (2022). Taxing top incomes in a world of ideas. Journal of Political Economy, 130(9), 2227-2274.




X. X. Sala-I-Martin. I just ran two million regressions. American Economic Review Papers and Proceedings, 87(2):178–183, 1997.
J. Temple. The new growth evidence. Journal of economic Literature, 37(1):112–156, 1999.





J. Benhabib and M. M. Spiegel. The role of human capital in economic development evidence from aggregate cross-country data. Journal of Monetary economics, 34(2):143–173, May 1994.
Bils, M., & Klenow, P. J. (2000). Does schooling cause growth?. American economic review, 90(5), 1160-1183.
Hanushek, E. A., & Woessmann, L. (2012). Do better schools lead to more growth? Cognitive skills, economic outcomes, and causation. Journal of economic growth, 17(4), 267-321.
Barro, R. J., & Lee, J. W. (2013). A new data set of educational attainment in the world, 1950–2010. Journal of development economics, 104, 184-198.
Valero, A., & Van Reenen, J. (2019). The economic impact of universities: Evidence from across the globe. Economics of education review, 68, 53-67.


The university literature is interesting because of the changing nature of work and whether it will make the univeristy system obsolete.





The papers by Romer and Lucas (On Mechanics of Economic Development) are the seminal papers in this literature.


Aghion, P., & Howitt, P. (1992). A model of growth through creative destruction. Econometrica: Journal of the Econometric Society, 323-351.
Jones, C. I. (1995). R & D-based models of economic growth. Journal of political Economy, 103(4), 759-784.
Acemoglu, D. (2002). Directed technical change. The review of economic studies, 69(4), 781-809.





Acemoglu, D., Aghion, P., Bursztyn, L., & Hemous, D. (2012). The environment and directed technical change. American economic review, 102(1), 131-166.


This paper is interesting in the sense that it pushes the endogenous growth literature, which was narrowed into directed technical change, into a new direction by linking it to the environment. The paper is not explosive in the sense that it is not a new idea but it is important in the sense that it is pushing the literature in a new direction.


Hassler, J., Krusell, P., & Olovsson, C. (2021). Directed technical change as a response to natural resource scarcity. Journal of Political Economy, 129(11), 3039-3072.





D. Acemoglu, P. Aghion, and F. Zilibotti. Distance to frontier, selection, and economic growth. Journal of the European Economic association, 4(1):37–74, 2006.


Growth mechanisms differ by:distance to frontier. If an economy is far from the frontier → imitation. If an economy is close to the frontier → innovation.





Acemoglu, D., Johnson, S., & Robinson, J. A. (2001). The colonial origins of comparative development: An empirical investigation. American economic review, 91(5), 1369-1401.


This paper is interesting because of the way it links the colonial history of a country to its current economic performance through the channel of institutions. It proposes a novel instrument for institutions and brings an interesting discussion on the role of institutions in economic development.


Rodrik, D., Subramanian, A., & Trebbi, F. (2004). Institutions rule: the primacy of institutions over geography and integration in economic development. Journal of economic growth, 9(2), 131-165.





Countries are not poor because they lack capital—they are poor because they use capital inefficiently.


Hsieh, C. T., & Klenow, P. J. (2009). Misallocation and manufacturing TFP in China and India. The Quarterly journal of economics, 124(4), 1403-1448.
Restuccia, D., & Rogerson, R. (2008). Policy distortions and aggregate productivity with heterogeneous establishments. Review of Economic dynamics, 11(4), 707-720.


In an efficient economy, we have high productive firms that are large and low productive firms that are small. However, with distortions such as taxes, subsidies, regulations, and entry barriers, we have productive firms that are too small and unproductive firms that are too large. This leads to a fall in aggregate output.
